# capnpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnpc/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#capn-proto-schema-compiler-plugin-library)Cap’n Proto Schema Compiler Plugin Library

This library allows you to do
[Cap’n Proto code generation](https://capnproto.org/otherlang.html#how-to-write-compiler-plugins)
within a Cargo build. You still need the `capnp` binary (implemented in C++).
(If you use a package manager, try looking for a package called
`capnproto`.)

In your Cargo.toml:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
[dependencies]
capnp = "0.26" # Note this is a different library than capnp*c*
[build-dependencies]
capnpc = "0.26"
```
In your build.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    capnpc::CompilerCommand::new()
        .src_prefix("schema")
        .file("schema/foo.capnp")
        .file("schema/bar.capnp")
        .run().expect("schema compiler command");
}
```
In your lib.rs:

This will be equivalent to executing the shell command

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compiler](https://docs.rs/struct.CompilerCommand.html)- Command
- A builder object for schema compiler commands.

[§](https://docs.rs#capn-proto-schema-compiler-plugin-library)Cap’n Proto Schema Compiler Plugin Library

within a Cargo build. You still need the `capnp` binary (implemented in C++).
(If you use a package manager, try looking for a package called

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    capnpc::CompilerCommand::new()
        .src_prefix("schema")

        .file("schema/bar.capnp")

# capnpc 0.26.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnpc/latest

# Cap'n Proto code generation for Rust

The generated code depends on the [capnproto-rust runtime library](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust).

Code generation can be customized through the annotations defined in [ rust.capnp](https://docs.rs/rust.capnp).

# capnp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp/^0.26.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#capn-proto-runtime-library)Cap’n Proto Runtime Library

This crate contains basic facilities for reading and writing
[Cap’n Proto](https://capnproto.org) messages in Rust. It is intended to
be used in conjunction with code generated by the
[capnpc-rust](https://crates.io/crates/capnpc) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [any_](https://docs.rs/any_pointer/index.html)- pointer
- Untyped pointer that can be cast to any struct, list, or capability type.
- [any_](https://docs.rs/any_pointer_list/index.html)- pointer_ - list
- List of AnyPointers.
- [capability](https://docs.rs/capability/index.html)
- Hooks for the RPC system.
- [capability_](https://docs.rs/capability_list/index.html)- list
- List of capabilities.
- [constant](https://docs.rs/constant/index.html)
- Helper type for generated Struct and List constants.
- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)
- Sequence of bytes.
- [data_](https://docs.rs/data_list/index.html)- list
- List of sequences of bytes.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_list/index.html)- list
- Dynamically-typed lists.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_struct/index.html)- struct
- Dynamically-typed structs.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_value/index.html)- value
- Dynamically typed values.
- [enum_](https://docs.rs/enum_list/index.html)- list
- List of enums.
- [introspect](https://docs.rs/introspect/index.html)
- Traits and types to support run-time type introspection, i.e. reflection.
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Custom I/O traits that roughly mirror `std::io::{Read, BufRead, Write}`. This extra layer of indirection enables support of no-std environments.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/list_list/index.html)- list
- List of lists.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- Untyped root container for a Cap’n Proto value.
- [primitive_](https://docs.rs/primitive_list/index.html)- list
- List of primitives.
- [private](https://docs.rs/private/index.html)
- Implementation details that should never be directly used by clients.
- [raw](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html)
- Functions providing low level access to encoded data.
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Convenience wrappers of the datatypes defined in schema.capnp.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_capnp/index.html)- capnp
- Code generated from
[schema.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/schema.capnp).
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serialize/index.html)
- Reading and writing of messages using the
[standard stream framing](https://capnproto.org/encoding.html#serialization-over-a-stream).
- [serialize_](https://docs.rs/serialize_packed/index.html)- packed
- Reading and writing of messages using the
[packed stream encoding](https://capnproto.org/encoding.html#packing).
- [struct_](https://docs.rs/struct_list/index.html)- list
- List of structs.
- [text](https://docs.rs/text/index.html)
- UTF-8 encoded text.
- [text_](https://docs.rs/text_list/index.html)- list
- List of strings containing UTF-8 encoded text.
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [generated_](https://docs.rs/macro.generated_code.html)- code
- Macro for importing Rust code that has been generated by `capnpc::CompilerCommand`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Describes an arbitrary error that prevented an operation from completing.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageSize.html)- Size
- Size of a message. Every generated struct has a method `.total_size()`that returns this.
- [NotIn](https://docs.rs/struct.NotInSchema.html)- Schema
- An enum value or union discriminant that was not found among those defined in a schema.
- [Word](https://docs.rs/struct.Word.html)
- 8 bytes, aligned to an 8-byte boundary.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- The general nature of an error. The purpose of this enum is not to describe the error itself, but rather to describe how the client might want to respond to the error.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/enum.OutputSegments.html)- Segments
- Helper struct that allows `MessageBuilder::get_segments_for_output()`to avoid heap allocations in the single-segment case.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [word](https://docs.rs/fn.word.html)
- Constructs a word with the given bytes.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Because messages are lazily validated, the return type of any method that reads a pointer field must be wrapped in a Result.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# sandogasa_koji - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandogasa-koji/0.15.3/sandogasa_koji/

## Expand description

Koji build system CLI wrapper.

Provides functions for querying Koji tags and builds by shelling
out to the `koji` CLI. Supports multiple Koji profiles (e.g.
`cbs` for CentOS Build System).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [TagAdd](https://docs.rs/struct.TagAddEvent.html)- Event
- One “tagged into” event from `koji list-history --tag=<tag>`. Captures only the bits the activity-reporting code needs; the date column is parsed by the caller as needed.
- [Tagged](https://docs.rs/struct.TaggedBuild.html)- Build
- A build found in a Koji tag.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_creation_date.html)- creation_ - date
- Parse the build’s creation date from `koji buildinfo`.
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_info_with_changelog.html)- info_ - with_ - changelog
- Fetch `koji buildinfo --changelog <nvr>`output verbatim for display. Returns the raw stdout so callers can show it to a human reviewing the build. Errors propagate (unlike the date/rpm helpers, an unexpected failure here is worth surfacing during an interactive review).
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_rpms.html)- rpms
- List binary RPM names for a build via `koji buildinfo`.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_auth.html)- auth
- Verify an authenticated Koji session is available for `profile`by running`koji moshimoshi`(the authenticated hello).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged.html)- tagged
- List builds in a Koji tag with their owners.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged_nvrs.html)- tagged_ - nvrs
- List NVRs in a Koji tag (quiet mode, NVRs only).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged_package_names.html)- tagged_ - package_ - names
- List the latest source package names tagged into a Koji tag.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tags.html)- tags
- List Koji tag names matching a glob `pattern`(e.g.`hyperscale10s-*-release`). Wraps`koji list-tags <pattern>`.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_nvr.html)- nvr
- Parse an NVR string into (name, version, release).
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_nvr_name.html)- nvr_ - name
- Parse an NVR string into the package name.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_tag_history.html)- tag_ - history
- Parse `koji list-history`output and pick out only the “tagged into” entries. Format of those lines (as of koji 1.34,`--utc`):
- [regen_](https://docs.rs/fn.regen_repo.html)- repo
- Regenerate a Koji tag’s repo (`koji regen-repo --wait <tag>`).
- [tag_](https://docs.rs/fn.tag_build.html)- build
- Tag a build into a Koji tag (`koji tag-build --wait <tag> <nvr>`).
- [tag_](https://docs.rs/fn.tag_history.html)- history
- Walk a tag’s “tagged into” events in the window `[after, before)`and return them in chronological order. Implemented via`koji list-history --tag=<tag>`parsed line-by-line; only`tagged into`lines are kept (other event types like owner changes and untags are filtered out).
- [untag_](https://docs.rs/fn.untag_build.html)- build
- Untag a build from a Koji tag (`koji untag-build <tag> <nvr>`).

---

# hrdr_tools - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-tools/0.2.1/hrdr_tools/

## Expand description

`hrdr-tools` — the agentic tool set.

The locked MVP set: `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit`, `bash`, `grep`,
`glob`, `todo_write`. Each implements [ Tool](https://docs.rs/trait.Tool.html) and is exposed to the model
as a native OpenAI function. Efficiency is in the design: token-bounded
outputs, line-numbered reads for precise edits, ripgrep-backed search.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Bash](https://docs.rs/struct.BashTool.html)- Tool
- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.CheckpointInfo.html)- Info
- One revertible checkpoint (a turn that changed files).
- [Checkpoints](https://docs.rs/struct.Checkpoints.html)
- A disk-backed store of per-turn file pre-images.
- [Edit](https://docs.rs/struct.EditTool.html)- Tool
- [Glob](https://docs.rs/struct.GlobTool.html)- Tool
- [Grep](https://docs.rs/struct.GrepTool.html)- Tool
- [Guardrail](https://docs.rs/struct.Guardrail.html)
- One command rule: a regex matched against the whole shell command line and the corrective message returned to the model when it matches.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/struct.Hook.html)
- One configured hook: run `run`(with`{path}`substituted) after tool`on`successfully mutates a file matching`glob`.
- [Power](https://docs.rs/struct.PowerShellTool.html)- Shell - Tool
- [Read](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadTool.html)- Tool
- [Todo](https://docs.rs/struct.TodoItem.html)- Item
- A single TODO item tracked by `todo_write`.
- [Todo](https://docs.rs/struct.TodoTool.html)- Tool
- [Tool](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolContext.html)- Context
- Shared execution context handed to every tool call.
- [Tool](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolRegistry.html)- Registry
- Ordered registry of tools, keyed by name.
- [WebFetch](https://docs.rs/struct.WebFetchTool.html)- Tool
- [WebSearch](https://docs.rs/struct.WebSearchTool.html)- Tool
- [Write](https://docs.rs/struct.WriteTool.html)- Tool

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS.html)- HOOK_ - TIMEOUT_ - MS
- Default per-hook timeout: formatters are fast; anything slower is stuck.
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT.html)- MAX_ - OUTPUT
- Default cap on a single tool’s textual output, in bytes. Larger results are truncated with a marker so the model’s context is never blown by one call.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Tool](https://docs.rs/trait.Tool.html)
- A model-callable tool.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [available_](https://docs.rs/fn.available_shell_tools.html)- shell_ - tools
- The available shell tools for this machine (bash and/or PowerShell), only
including a tool when its interpreter is actually on `PATH`.
- [cap_](https://docs.rs/fn.cap_matches.html)- matches
- Cap search output at `max_matches`*matches*, appending a count of what was dropped and how to narrow the search. Only`path:NN:…`lines count as matches —`path-NN-…`context lines and`--`group separators (grep/rg`-C`format) ride along with their match, so a context-grep isn’t over-counted.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_guardrails.html)- guardrails
- First matching rule’s message, if `command`trips any guardrail. Quoted spans are blanked before matching so string*arguments*that merely mention a blocked command (e.g.`rg 'git add -A'`) don’t false-positive.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_guardrails.html)- guardrails
- The built-in rules. Patterns are matched anywhere in the command string
(compound `a && b`commands included). Kept deliberately narrow: they block the exact foot-gun spellings, not whole subcommands.
- [floor_](https://docs.rs/fn.floor_char_boundary.html)- char_ - boundary
- Largest byte index `≤ max`that lies on a UTF-8 char boundary of`s`, so`&s[..floor_char_boundary(s, max)]`never panics on multibyte text. Returns`s.len()`when`max >= s.len()`. (std’s`str::floor_char_boundary`is still unstable, hence this helper.)
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_file_hooks.html)- file_ - hooks
- Run every hook matching (`tool`,`path`) sequentially, returning one warning line per hook that failed or timed out (empty = all quiet). Success output is discarded — the caller re-reads the file and diffs, so the model sees the effect, not the chatter.
- [truncate](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate.html)
- Truncate `text`to`max`bytes on a char boundary, appending a marker that tells the model output was cut.
- [truncate_](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate_inline.html)- inline
- Collapse `s`to a single line (newlines → spaces) and truncate to`max`**characters**, appending`…`if it was cut. For compact one-line previews (tool-arg previews, status lines) — width-based, unlike the byte-based`truncate`
- [truncate_](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate_middle.html)- middle
- Truncate to `max`bytes keeping the**head and tail**with the omission in the middle. For shell output: build/test runs put the errors at the end, so head-only truncation (plain`truncate`
- [unix_](https://docs.rs/fn.unix_now.html)- now
- Current Unix time in whole seconds (0 if the clock is before the epoch). Shared by checkpoint journaling and session metadata.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Assignee](https://docs.rs/struct.Assignee.html)

- Client for the GitLab REST API v4.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)
- One entry from the user-activity events endpoint. Fields are
sparse — GitLab only populates the ones relevant to each
`action_name`.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.EventNote.html)- Note
- Note payload attached to `commented on`events.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.EventPushData.html)- Push - Data
- Push payload attached to `pushed to`/`pushed new`events.

- Client for group-level GitLab API queries.

- A GitLab merge request (minimal fields).

- A project’s status flags relevant to filing issues. Fetched from the project endpoint; the issue-feature flags only appear for authenticated requests.
- [Project](https://docs.rs/struct.ProjectSummary.html)- Summary

`path_with_namespace`prefix and render a human-readable link.

- Author block on a Release. Username is the field most useful for cross-referencing with the calling user’s profile.
- [Release](https://docs.rs/struct.ReleaseLinks.html)- Links

- [Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html)

- [User](https://docs.rs/struct.User.html)
- A GitLab user as returned by `/users?username=<name>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [count_](https://docs.rs/fn.count_authored_commits.html)- authored_ - commits
- Count commits in `project_id`authored by`author`within`[since, until]`(inclusive). GitLab’s commits endpoint matches the`author`parameter against both name and email fields, so passing the GitLab username usually works; if the user authored commits under an email only, pass that email string instead.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_archived_project_names.html)- archived_ - project_ - names
- List the **archived**projects under a GitLab group, returning their names. GitLab’s`archived=true`filter narrows the listing server-side, so this is a cheap separate query rather than enriching every project in the main listing.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_group_projects.html)- group_ - projects
- List all projects under a GitLab group (public, no auth needed).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tags.html)- tags
- List tags for a project, paginated. Returns an empty list on
404. Uses `order_by=updated&sort=desc`so newer tags come first — handy when the caller wants to short-circuit on the first tag older than its window of interest.
- [package_](https://docs.rs/fn.package_from_issue_url.html)- from_ - issue_ - url
- Extract the package name from a GitLab issue or work item web_url.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_issue_url.html)- issue_ - url
- Parse a GitLab issue / work-item URL into its components.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_mr_url.html)- mr_ - url
- Parse a merge request URL into its components.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_project_url.html)- project_ - url
- Parse a GitLab project URL into (base_url, project_path).
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_path_from_issue_url.html)- path_ - from_ - issue_ - url
- Extract the project path from a GitLab issue or work item web_url.
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_releases.html)- releases
- List releases for a project. Returns an empty list on 404 (project gone) so callers can iterate over many projects without per-project error handling.
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_summary.html)- summary
- Look up a project’s `path_with_namespace`from its numeric ID. Used to map event`project_id`→ group-prefix filter.
- [user_](https://docs.rs/fn.user_by_username.html)- by_ - username
- Look up a user by username on a specific GitLab instance.
Returns `Ok(None)`if the server returns 200 with an empty list (no user with that name on that instance).
- [user_](https://docs.rs/fn.user_events.html)- events
- Fetch a user’s activity events within `[after, before)`— GitLab’s event endpoint is half-open on both sides and rejects both-null. Results are paginated at 100/page; this follows every page until a short page arrives.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_token.html)- token
- Check whether a token is valid by calling `GET /api/v4/user`.

# sandogasa_github - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandogasa-github/0.15.3/sandogasa_github/

## Expand description

HTTP client for the GitHub REST API.

Scoped to the surface `sandogasa-report` needs for activity
reports: user identity lookup, token validation, paginated
user events (to find which repos a user touched in a window),
the Search API for pull requests, and per-repo
authored-commit counts.

Mirrors `sandogasa-gitlab` in shape so downstream tools can
treat the two forges the same way structurally — host-keyed
tokens and identities, optional org/group filter, etc.

```
use sandogasa_github::Client;
let client = Client::new("https://api.github.com", "ghp_token")?;
let user = client.user_by_username("octocat")?.expect("user exists");
let prs = client.search_pull_requests(
    &format!("type:pr author:{} created:2026-01-01..2026-03-31", user.login),
)?;
for pr in prs {
    println!("{}: {}", pr.number, pr.title);
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Annotated](https://docs.rs/struct.AnnotatedTag.html)- Tag
- An annotated-tag object from
`/repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/tags/{sha}`. Only annotated tags carry tagger metadata; lightweight tags don’t have an addressable tag object.
- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)
- Blocking GitHub REST client.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)
- One entry from `/users/{username}/events`. Fields are sparse; we keep just enough to identify the event type, associated repo, and the actor.
- [GitObject](https://docs.rs/struct.GitObject.html)
- The thing a Git ref points at. `object_type`is`"commit"`for lightweight tags and`"tag"`for annotated ones.
- [GitTag](https://docs.rs/struct.GitTagRef.html)- Ref
- One entry from `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/refs/tags`. The underlying`object`distinguishes lightweight tags (point directly to a commit) from annotated tags (point to a Tag object that carries tagger info).
- [Pull](https://docs.rs/struct.PullRequest.html)- Request
- A pull request as returned by the Search Issues endpoint
when filtering on `type:pr`. The Search API actually returns “issue” objects with PR-specific fields populated, so we shape this around the union of useful fields rather than the fuller`/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}`model.
- [Pull](https://docs.rs/struct.PullRequestRef.html)- Request - Ref
- Auxiliary block on a search-result issue when it’s actually a pull request. The Search Issues endpoint signals “is PR” by populating this; merged state lives here too.
- [Repository](https://docs.rs/struct.Repository.html)
- A repository as returned by event payloads and PR responses.
- [Tagger](https://docs.rs/struct.Tagger.html)
- `name`+- `email`+- `date`triple stamped on annotated-tag creation.- `date`is ISO 8601 (e.g.- `2026-05-15T17:03:15Z`).
- [User](https://docs.rs/struct.User.html)
- A GitHub user as returned by `/users/{username}`. Only the fields downstream tools currently consume.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_BASE_URL.html)- BASE_ - URL
- Default production base URL for the GitHub REST API.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_token.html)- token
- Check whether `token`works against`base_url`by hitting`/user`. Returns`Ok(true)`for valid tokens,`Ok(false)`for 401s, and`Err`for other transport / server errors so callers can distinguish “tried and was rejected” from “couldn’t reach the server”.

# sandogasa_forgejo - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandogasa-forgejo/0.15.3/sandogasa_forgejo/

## Expand description

HTTP client for the Forgejo / Gitea REST API (v1).

Forgejo (and the Gitea it forks) expose a GitHub-ish REST API rooted
at `<instance>/api/v1`. This crate covers the surface two sandogasa
tools need:

- `sandogasa-report`’s merged-PR accounting — the pull requests the authenticated token owner created, across- *every*repo they contribute to (not just their own org), via the global issue/pull search (- `Client::my_pull_requests`
- `ebranch`’s releng-ticket filing —- `Client::create_issue`- `Client::search_issues`

The instance host is always passed in full, so it works against any
deployment — codeberg.org, a Fedora Forgejo, a self-hosted Gitea.
Mirrors `sandogasa-github`/`sandogasa-gitlab` in shape so downstream
tools can treat the forges the same way structurally (host-keyed
tokens and identities, an optional owner/org filter, etc.).

Because the global search filters by `created=true` (the token
owner), the client reports the activity of *whoever owns the token* —
which is exactly the self-reporting use case. Point it at your own
instance token.

```
use sandogasa_forgejo::Client;
let client = Client::new("https://codeberg.org", "token")?;
for pr in client.my_pull_requests("closed", None)? {
    if pr.is_merged() {
        println!("{}#{} {}", pr.repo_slug().unwrap_or(""), pr.number, pr.title);
    }
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)
- A Forgejo / Gitea API client bound to one instance.
- [GitRef](https://docs.rs/struct.GitRef.html)
- A git ref (branch or commit) as embedded in a pull request’s
`head`/`base`.
- [Issue](https://docs.rs/struct.Issue.html)
- An issue — from either the per-repo issue endpoints (create/search)
or the global issue search. The richer fields (`created_at`,`closed_at`,`repository`) are populated by the search; the per-repo endpoints leave them at their defaults.
- [Pull](https://docs.rs/struct.PullDetail.html)- Detail
- The fuller pull-request object (`/pulls/{n}`) — the head/base refs the issue/pull*search*result omits. Needed to tell whether a closed-but-unmerged PR’s commit nonetheless landed on the target branch (applied out-of-band).
- [Pull](https://docs.rs/struct.PullInfo.html)- Info
- The `pull_request`sub-object on a search result — the bits that distinguish a merged PR from a merely-closed one.
- [Pull](https://docs.rs/struct.PullRequest.html)- Request
- A pull request as returned by the issue/pull search endpoint (an
issue object whose `pull_request`field is populated).
- [Repository](https://docs.rs/struct.RepositoryRef.html)- Ref
- The repository reference embedded in a pull-request search result.
In this compact form `owner`is a bare login string (not a full user object).
- [User](https://docs.rs/struct.User.html)
- A Forgejo user as returned by `/api/v1/user`. Only the fields downstream tools currently consume.
- [UserRef](https://docs.rs/struct.UserRef.html)
- The user reference embedded in a pull-request search result.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_token.html)- token
- Check whether a token is accepted by the instance, hitting
`/api/v1/user`.`Ok(true)`for a valid token,`Ok(false)`for 401,`Err`for anything else (so callers can tell “rejected” from “couldn’t reach the server”).

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

# polkadot_node_core_backing - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-core-backing/32.0.0/polkadot_node_core_backing/

## Expand description

Implements the `CandidateBackingSubsystem`.

This subsystem maintains the entire responsibility of tracking parachain candidates which can be backed, as well as the issuance of statements about candidates when run on a validator node.

There are two types of statements: `Seconded` and `Valid`.
`Seconded` implies `Valid`, and nothing should be stated as
`Valid` unless its already been `Seconded`.

Validators may only second candidates which fall under their own group
assignment, and they may only second one candidate per depth per active leaf.
Candidates which are stated as either `Second` or `Valid` by a majority of the
assigned group of validators may be backed on-chain and proceed to the availability
stage.

Depth is a concept relating to asynchronous backing, by which short sub-chains of candidates are backed and extended off-chain, and then placed asynchronously into blocks of the relay chain as those are authored and as the relay-chain state becomes ready for them. Asynchronous backing allows parachains to grow mostly independently from the state of the relay chain, which gives more time for parachains to be validated and thereby increases performance.

Most of the work of asynchronous backing is handled by the Prospective Parachains subsystem. The ‘depth’ of a parachain block with respect to a relay chain block is a measure of how many parachain blocks are between the most recent included parachain block in the post-state of the relay-chain block and the candidate. For instance, a candidate that descends directly from the most recent parachain block in the relay-chain state has depth 0. The child of that candidate would have depth 1. And so on.

The candidate backing subsystem keeps track of a set of ‘active leaves’ which are the most recent blocks in the relay-chain (which is in fact a tree) which could be built upon. Depth is always measured against active leaves, and the valid relay-parent that each candidate can have is determined by the active leaves. The Prospective Parachains subsystem enforces that the relay-parent increases monotonically, so that logic is not handled here. By communicating with the Prospective Parachains subsystem, this subsystem extrapolates an “implicit view” from the set of currently active leaves, which determines the set of all recent relay-chain block hashes which could be relay-parents for candidates backed in children of the active leaves.

In fact, this subsystem relies on the Statement Distribution subsystem to prevent spam by enforcing the rule that each validator may second at most one candidate per depth per active leaf. This bounds the number of candidates that the system needs to consider and is not handled within this subsystem, except for candidates seconded locally.

This subsystem also handles relay-chain heads which don’t support asynchronous backing. For such active leaves, the only valid relay-parent is the leaf hash itself and the only allowed depth is 0.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Candidate](https://docs.rs/struct.CandidateBackingSubsystem.html)- Backing - Subsystem
- The candidate backing subsystem.

# camel_dataformat_protobuf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-dataformat-protobuf/0.22.0/camel_dataformat_protobuf/

## Expand description

camel-dataformat-protobuf — Protobuf DataFormat for Apache Camel Rust.

Provides marshal/unmarshal support for Protocol Buffers using dynamic message
descriptors compiled at runtime via `prost-reflect`. JSON ↔ binary protobuf
round-tripping is supported out of the box.

TODO(PROTO-005): Schema registry integration (e.g. Confluent Schema Registry) is not yet implemented. When available, this will allow automatic schema lookup/registration by subject and version during marshal/unmarshal.

# capnpc 0.26.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnpc/0.26.0

# Cap'n Proto code generation for Rust

The generated code depends on the [capnproto-rust runtime library](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust).

Code generation can be customized through the annotations defined in [ rust.capnp](https://docs.rs/rust.capnp).

# capnpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnpc/0.26.0/target-redirect/capnpc/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#capn-proto-schema-compiler-plugin-library)Cap’n Proto Schema Compiler Plugin Library

This library allows you to do
[Cap’n Proto code generation](https://capnproto.org/otherlang.html#how-to-write-compiler-plugins)
within a Cargo build. You still need the `capnp` binary (implemented in C++).
(If you use a package manager, try looking for a package called
`capnproto`.)

In your Cargo.toml:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
[dependencies]
capnp = "0.26" # Note this is a different library than capnp*c*
[build-dependencies]
capnpc = "0.26"
```
In your build.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    capnpc::CompilerCommand::new()
        .src_prefix("schema")
        .file("schema/foo.capnp")
        .file("schema/bar.capnp")
        .run().expect("schema compiler command");
}
```
In your lib.rs:

This will be equivalent to executing the shell command

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compiler](https://docs.rs/struct.CompilerCommand.html)- Command
- A builder object for schema compiler commands.

[74](https://docs.rs#74)// Copied from capnp/src/lib.rs, where this conversion lives behind the "std" feature flag,
[75](https://docs.rs#75)// which we don't want to depend on here.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)pub(crate) fn convert_io_err(err: std::io::Error) -> capnp::Error {
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    use std::io;
[78](https://docs.rs#78)    let kind = match err.kind() {
[79](https://docs.rs#79)        io::ErrorKind::TimedOut => capnp::ErrorKind::Overloaded,
[80](https://docs.rs#80)        io::ErrorKind::BrokenPipe
[81](https://docs.rs#81)        | io::ErrorKind::ConnectionRefused
[82](https://docs.rs#82)        | io::ErrorKind::ConnectionReset
[83](https://docs.rs#83)        | io::ErrorKind::ConnectionAborted
[84](https://docs.rs#84)        | io::ErrorKind::NotConnected => capnp::ErrorKind::Disconnected,
[85](https://docs.rs#85)        _ => capnp::ErrorKind::Failed,
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    };
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    capnp::Error {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)        extra: format!("{err}"),
[89](https://docs.rs#89)        kind,
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    }
[91](https://docs.rs#91)}
[92](https://docs.rs#92)
[93](https://docs.rs#93)fn run_command(
[94](https://docs.rs#94)    mut command: ::std::process::Command,
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    mut code_generation_command: codegen::CodeGenerationCommand,
[96](https://docs.rs#96)) -> ::capnp::Result<()> {
[97](https://docs.rs#97)    let mut p = command.spawn().map_err(convert_io_err)?;
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    code_generation_command.run(p.stdout.take().unwrap())?;
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    let exit_status = p.wait().map_err(convert_io_err)?;
[100](https://docs.rs#100)    if !exit_status.success() {
[101](https://docs.rs#101)        Err(::capnp::Error::failed(format!(
[102](https://docs.rs#102)            "Non-success exit status: {exit_status}"
[103](https://docs.rs#103)        )))
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    } else {
[105](https://docs.rs#105)        Ok(())
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    }
[107](https://docs.rs#107)}

[158](https://docs.rs#158)    /// Specify that `crate_name` provides generated code for `files`.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    ///
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    /// This means that when your schema refers to types defined in `files` we
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    /// will generate Rust code that uses identifiers in `crate_name`.
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    ///
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    /// # Arguments
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    ///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// - `crate_name`: The Rust identifier of the crate
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// - `files`: the Capnp file ids the crate provides generated code for
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    ///
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// # When to use
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    ///
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// You only need this when your generated code needs to refer to types in
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// the external crate. If you just want to use an annotation and the
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// argument to that annotation is a builtin type (e.g. `$Json.name`) this
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    /// isn't necessary.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    ///
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// # Example
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    ///
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// If you write a schema like so
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    ///
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// ```capnp
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// // my_schema.capnp
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    ///
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// using Json = import "/capnp/compat/json.capnp";
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    ///
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// struct Foo {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    ///     value @0 :Json.Value;
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// }
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    /// ```
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    ///
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    /// you'd look at [json.capnp][json.capnp] to see its capnp id.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    ///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// ```capnp
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// // json.capnp
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    ///
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    /// # Copyright (c) 2015 Sandstorm Development Group, Inc. and contributors ...
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// @0x8ef99297a43a5e34;
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// ```
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    ///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// If you want the `foo::Builder::get_value` method generated for your
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// schema to return a `capnp_json::json_capnp::value::Reader` you'd add a
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// dependency on `capnp_json` to your `Cargo.toml` and specify it provides
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    /// `json.capnp` in your `build.rs`.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    ///
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// ```rust,no_run
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// // build.rs
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ///
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// capnpc::CompilerCommand::new()
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    ///     .crate_provides("json_capnp", [0x8ef99297a43a5e34])
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    ///     .file("my_schema.capnp")
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    ///     .run()
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    ///     .unwrap();
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// ```
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    ///
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// [json.capnp]:
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    ///     https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/compat/json.capnp
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    pub fn crate_provides(
[216](https://docs.rs#216)        &mut self,
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        crate_name: impl Into<String>,
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        files: impl IntoIterator<Item = u64>,
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    ) -> &mut Self {
[220](https://docs.rs#220)        let crate_name = crate_name.into();
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        for file in files.into_iter() {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)            self.crate_provides_map.insert(file, crate_name.clone());
[223](https://docs.rs#223)        }
[224](https://docs.rs#224)        self
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    }
[226](https://docs.rs#226)

[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    /// Internal function for starting to build a capnp command.
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    fn new_command(&self) -> ::std::process::Command {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        if let Some(executable) = &self.executable_path {
[256](https://docs.rs#256)            ::std::process::Command::new(executable)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        } else {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            ::std::process::Command::new("capnp")
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        }
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// Sets the default parent module. This indicates the scope in your crate where you will
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// add a module containing the generated code. For example, if you set this option to
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// `vec!["foo".into(), "bar".into()]`, and you are generating code for `baz.capnp`, then your crate
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// should have this structure:
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    ///
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// ```ignore
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    /// pub mod foo {
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    ///    pub mod bar {
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    ///        pub mod baz_capnp {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    ///            include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/baz_capnp.rs"));
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    ///        }
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    ///    }
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// }
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// ```
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    ///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// This option can be overridden by the `parentModule` annotation defined in `rust.capnp`.
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    ///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// If this option is unset, the default is the crate root.
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    pub fn default_parent_module(&mut self, default_parent_module: Vec<String>) -> &mut Self {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        self.default_parent_module = default_parent_module;
[282](https://docs.rs#282)        self
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    }
[284](https://docs.rs#284)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    /// If set, the generator will also write a file containing the raw code generator request to the
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// specified path.
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    pub fn raw_code_generator_request_path<P>(&mut self, path: P) -> &mut Self
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    where
[289](https://docs.rs#289)        P: AsRef<Path>,
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        self.raw_code_generator_request_path = Some(path.as_ref().to_path_buf());
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        self
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    }
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// Runs the command.
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// Returns an error if `OUT_DIR` or a custom output directory was not set, or if `capnp compile` fails.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    pub fn run(&mut self) -> ::capnp::Result<()> {
[298](https://docs.rs#298)        match self.new_command().arg("--version").output() {
[299](https://docs.rs#299)            Err(error) => {
[300](https://docs.rs#300)                return Err(::capnp::Error::failed(format!(
[301](https://docs.rs#301)                    "Failed to execute `capnp --version`: {error}. \
[302](https://docs.rs#302)                     Please verify that version 0.5.2 or higher of the capnp executable \
[303](https://docs.rs#303)                     is installed on your system. See https://capnproto.org/install.html"
[304](https://docs.rs#304)                )))
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            }
[306](https://docs.rs#306)            Ok(output) => {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)                if !output.status.success() {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)                    return Err(::capnp::Error::failed(format!(
[309](https://docs.rs#309)                        "`capnp --version` returned an error: {:?}. \
[310](https://docs.rs#310)                         Please verify that version 0.5.2 or higher of the capnp executable \
[311](https://docs.rs#311)                         is installed on your system. See https://capnproto.org/install.html",
[312](https://docs.rs#312)                        output.status
[313](https://docs.rs#313)                    )));
[314](https://docs.rs#314)                }
[315](https://docs.rs#315)                // TODO Parse the version string?
[316](https://docs.rs#316)            }
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        }
[318](https://docs.rs#318)
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        let mut command = self.new_command();
[320](https://docs.rs#320)
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        // We remove PWD from the env to avoid the following warning.
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        // kj/filesystem-disk-unix.c++:1690:
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        //    warning: PWD environment variable doesn't match current directory
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        command.env_remove("PWD");
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        command.arg("compile").arg("-o").arg("-");
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        if self.no_standard_import {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)            command.arg("--no-standard-import");
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        for import_path in &self.import_paths {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            command.arg(format!("--import-path={}", import_path.display()));
[334](https://docs.rs#334)        }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        for src_prefix in &self.src_prefixes {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            command.arg(format!("--src-prefix={}", src_prefix.display()));
[338](https://docs.rs#338)        }
[339](https://docs.rs#339)
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        for file in &self.files {
[341](https://docs.rs#341)            std::fs::metadata(file).map_err(|error| {
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                let current_dir = match std::env::current_dir() {
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                    Ok(current_dir) => format!("`{}`", current_dir.display()),
[344](https://docs.rs#344)                    Err(..) => "<unknown working directory>".to_string(),
[345](https://docs.rs#345)                };
[346](https://docs.rs#346)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)                ::capnp::Error::failed(format!(
[348](https://docs.rs#348)                    "Unable to stat capnp input file `{}` in working directory {}: {}.  \
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                     Please check that the file exists and is accessible for read.",
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                    file.display(),
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                    current_dir,
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                    error
[353](https://docs.rs#353)                ))
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            })?;
[355](https://docs.rs#355)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            command.arg(file);
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        }
[358](https://docs.rs#358)
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        let output_path = if let Some(output_path) = &self.output_path {
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            output_path.clone()
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        } else {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            // Try `OUT_DIR` by default
[363](https://docs.rs#363)            PathBuf::from(::std::env::var("OUT_DIR").map_err(|error| {
[364](https://docs.rs#364)                ::capnp::Error::failed(format!(
[365](https://docs.rs#365)                    "Could not access `OUT_DIR` environment variable: {error}. \
[366](https://docs.rs#366)                     You might need to set it up or instead create your own output \
[367](https://docs.rs#367)                     structure using `CompilerCommand::output_path`"
[368](https://docs.rs#368)                ))
[369](https://docs.rs#369)            })?)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        };
[371](https://docs.rs#371)
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        command.stdout(::std::process::Stdio::piped());
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        command.stderr(::std::process::Stdio::inherit());
[374](https://docs.rs#374)
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        let mut code_generation_command = crate::codegen::CodeGenerationCommand::new();
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        code_generation_command
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            .output_directory(output_path)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)            .default_parent_module(self.default_parent_module.clone())
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            .crates_provide_map(self.crate_provides_map.clone());
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        if let Some(raw_code_generator_request_path) = &self.raw_code_generator_request_path {
[381](https://docs.rs#381)            code_generation_command
[382](https://docs.rs#382)                .raw_code_generator_request_path(raw_code_generator_request_path.clone());
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        }
[384](https://docs.rs#384)
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        run_command(command, code_generation_command).map_err(|error| {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            ::capnp::Error::failed(format!(
[387](https://docs.rs#387)                "Error while trying to execute `capnp compile`: {error}."
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            ))
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        })
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)}
[392](https://docs.rs#392)
[393](https://docs.rs#393)#[test]
[394](https://docs.rs#394)#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]
[395](https://docs.rs#395)fn compiler_command_new_no_out_dir() {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    std::env::remove_var("OUT_DIR");
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    let error = CompilerCommand::new().run().unwrap_err().extra;
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    assert!(error.starts_with("Could not access `OUT_DIR` environment variable"));

Adds a –src-prefix flag. For all files specified for compilation that start
with `prefix`, removes the prefix when computing output filenames.

for absolute imports.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnpc/lib.rs.html#215-225)#### pub fn [crate_provides](https://docs.rs#method.crate_provides)(
    &mut self,
    crate_name: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>,
    files: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)>,
) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnpc/lib.rs.html#215-225)

#### pub fn [crate_provides](https://docs.rs#method.crate_provides)(
    &mut self,
    crate_name: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>,
    files: impl [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/collect/trait.IntoIterator.html)<Item = [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)>,
) -> &mut Self

Specify that `crate_name` provides generated code for `files`.

This means that when your schema refers to types defined in `files` we
will generate Rust code that uses identifiers in `crate_name`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `crate_name`: The Rust identifier of the crate
- `files`: the Capnp file ids the crate provides generated code for

[§](https://docs.rs#when-to-use)When to use

You only need this when your generated code needs to refer to types in
the external crate. If you just want to use an annotation and the
argument to that annotation is a builtin type (e.g. `$Json.name`) this
isn’t necessary.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

If you write a schema like so

```
// my_schema.capnp
using Json = import "/capnp/compat/json.capnp";
struct Foo {
    value @0 :Json.Value;
}
```
you’d look at [json.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/compat/json.capnp) to see its capnp id.

```
// json.capnp
# Copyright (c) 2015 Sandstorm Development Group, Inc. and contributors ...
@0x8ef99297a43a5e34;
```
If you want the `foo::Builder::get_value` method generated for your
schema to return a `capnp_json::json_capnp::value::Reader` you’d add a
dependency on `capnp_json` to your `Cargo.toml` and specify it provides
`json.capnp` in your `build.rs`.

```
// build.rs
capnpc::CompilerCommand::new()
    .crate_provides("json_capnp", [0x8ef99297a43a5e34])
    .file("my_schema.capnp")
    .run()
    .unwrap();
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnpc/lib.rs.html#229-232)#### pub fn [no_standard_import](https://docs.rs#method.no_standard_import)(&mut self) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnpc/lib.rs.html#229-232)

#### pub fn [no_standard_import](https://docs.rs#method.no_standard_import)(&mut self) -> &mut Self

Adds the –no-standard-import flag, indicating that the default import paths of /usr/include and /usr/local/include should not be included.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnpc/lib.rs.html#245-251)#### pub fn [capnp_executable](https://docs.rs#method.capnp_executable)<P>(&mut self, path: P) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnpc/lib.rs.html#245-251)

#### pub fn [capnp_executable](https://docs.rs#method.capnp_executable)<P>(&mut self, path: P) -> &mut Self

Specify the executable which is used for the ‘capnp’ tool. When this method is not called, the command looks for a name ‘capnp’ on the system (e.g. in working directory or in PATH environment variable).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnpc/lib.rs.html#280-283)#### pub fn [default_parent_module](https://docs.rs#method.default_parent_module)(
    &mut self,
    default_parent_module: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>,
) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnpc/lib.rs.html#280-283)

#### pub fn [default_parent_module](https://docs.rs#method.default_parent_module)(
    &mut self,
    default_parent_module: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>,
) -> &mut Self

Sets the default parent module. This indicates the scope in your crate where you will
add a module containing the generated code. For example, if you set this option to
`vec!["foo".into(), "bar".into()]`, and you are generating code for `baz.capnp`, then your crate
should have this structure:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
pub mod foo {
   pub mod bar {
       pub mod baz_capnp {
           include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/baz_capnp.rs"));
       }
   }
}
```
This option can be overridden by the `parentModule` annotation defined in `rust.capnp`.

If this option is unset, the default is the crate root.

# capnpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnpc/latest/capnpc/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#capn-proto-schema-compiler-plugin-library)Cap’n Proto Schema Compiler Plugin Library

This library allows you to do
[Cap’n Proto code generation](https://capnproto.org/otherlang.html#how-to-write-compiler-plugins)
within a Cargo build. You still need the `capnp` binary (implemented in C++).
(If you use a package manager, try looking for a package called
`capnproto`.)

In your Cargo.toml:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
[dependencies]
capnp = "0.26" # Note this is a different library than capnp*c*
[build-dependencies]
capnpc = "0.26"
```
In your build.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    capnpc::CompilerCommand::new()
        .src_prefix("schema")
        .file("schema/foo.capnp")
        .file("schema/bar.capnp")
        .run().expect("schema compiler command");
}
```
In your lib.rs:

This will be equivalent to executing the shell command

- A builder object for schema compiler commands.

# capnpc 0.26.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnpc/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# capnpc 0.25.3 - Docs.rs

# Cap'n Proto code generation for Rust

The generated code depends on the [capnproto-rust runtime library](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust).

Code generation can be customized through the annotations defined in [ rust.capnp](https://docs.rs/rust.capnp).

# capnpc 0.25.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnpc/0.25.0

# Cap'n Proto code generation for Rust

The generated code depends on the [capnproto-rust runtime library](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust).

Code generation can be customized through the annotations defined in [ rust.capnp](https://docs.rs/rust.capnp).

---

The generated code depends on the [capnproto-rust runtime library](https://github.com/dwrensha/capnproto-rust).

Documentation [here](http://docs.capnproto-rust.org/capnpc).

---

# capnpc 0.26.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnpc/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md

##v0.26.0-Adjust generated code for new RawEnumSchema constructor.
##v0.25.3-Avoid unreachable_pub warnings in generated code.
##v0.25.2-Use 4-space indents in generated code.
- Prefer TryFrom over TryInto in generated code.
##v0.25.1-Add version numbers in toplevel comment of generated code.
##v0.25.0-Use new GeneratedCodeArena to avoid need for `unsafe` in generated code.
##v0.24.1-Add local `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` annotations to generated code.
##v0.24.0-Adjust generated code to use new constructors for constants and RawStructSchema.
##v0.23.3-Adjust generated dispatch code to properly disambiguate when an 'extends' interface method
conflicts with another method.
##v0.23.2-Remove `async` block in generated code for streaming methods.
##v0.23.1-Use `f64::INFINITY` instead of `::core::f64::INFINITY` in generated code.
##v0.23.0-Update generated code of `Server` trait methods to take `self` as `Rc<Self>`.
##v0.22.0-Update generated code of `Server` traits to support `async fn` methods.
What previously was a `&mut self` parameter is now `&self`. Therefore
RPC objects must now add their own interior mutability as needed.
`Cell` or `RefCell` should suffice in most cases.
- Remove support for rustc editions older than 2021 (when `await` was added).
##v0.21.4-Update minimum required version of capnp base crate, to account for new
usage of impl Clone for capnp:: capability::Client.
##v0.21.3-Fix code generation for non-finite float point constants.
##v0.21.2-Use new `capability::DynClientHook` alias to avoid warnings in generated code.
##v0.21.1-Use new `introspect::panic_invalid_field_index()` and
`introspect::panic_invalid_annotation_indices()` functions so that
generated code can pass Clippy while still working on Rust 2015.
##v0.21.0-Follow v0.21.0 release of other capnp crates.
##v0.20.1-Elide more lifetimes in generated code to make Clippy happy.
##v0.20.0-Add support for `stream` keyword.
##v0.19.0-Include new members_by_name field of RawStructSchema.
- Generalize text, primitive_list, and enum_list setters using impl SetterInput.
##v0.18.1-Fix overly-restrictive lifetimes in setters of certain list fields.
##v0.18.0-Update for lazier utf-8 validation.
##v0.17.2-Add the `$Rust.option` annotation for declaring fields to be optional.
- Add `CompilerCommand::crate_provides()`, allowing cross-crate imports.
##v0.17.1-Fix setters of enum fields with defaults.
##v0.17.0-Add support for reflection.
- Implement `Debug` for all generated struct `Reader` types.
##v0.16.5-Use `core::marker` instead of `std::marker` for pointer constants, for no_std compat.
##v0.16.4-Generate explicit Clone and Copy impls for Reader structs.
- Fully-qualify `::capnp::Word` in generated code.
- Add `capnp --version` invocation before `capnp compile`, for better error reporting.
- Clear PWD env variable, to silence warning from kj/filesystem-disk-unix.c++.
##v0.16.3-Generate `*_has()` methods for capability fields.
##v0.16.2-Avoid ambiguous associated item in TryFrom implementations.
##v0.16.1-Fix clippy warnings in generated code.
##v0.16.0-Update code generation for removal of `To16`, `FromU16`, `FromStructReader`, `FromStructBuilder`.
##v0.15.2-Apply clippy lifetime elision suggestion in set_pointer_builder() in generated code.
##v0.15.1-Lots of style fixes and linting, including for generated code.
##v0.15.0-Support trait changes in capnp::traits.
- Remove deprecated function.
##v0.14.9-Fix Clippy warnings in generated code.
##v0.14.8-Include name of method in `unimplemented` error messages.
- Fix super interface lookup in case of transitive `extends` chain.
##v0.14.7-Canonicalize order of type parameters from the bugfix for issue 260.
##v0.14.6-Fix bug in code generation for unions that don't use all of their enclosing struct's generic params.
##v0.14.5-Fix bug in code generation for generic groups.
- Add CompilerCommand.raw_code_generator_request_path().
##v0.14.4-Check that schema files exist before attempting to invoke the schema compiler.
##v0.14.3-Include LICENSE in published crate.
##v0.14.2-Add CompilerCommand::default_parent_module() option.
- Add codegen::CodeGenerationCommand and deprecate codegen::generate_code().
##v0.14.1-Get generated code to pass the elided_lifetimes_in_paths lint.
##v0.14.0-Update for `SetPointerBuilder` no longer having a `To` type parameter.
- Make generated `Owned` structs unconstructable. They are only intented to be used as types, not values.
##v0.13.1-Fix some more clippy warnings in generated code.
##v0.13.0-Update to work without requiring "std" feature of capnp base crate.
- Refer to `core` instead of `std` in generated code.
- Remove deprecated `ToClient` structs from generated code.
##v0.12.4-Add `CompilerCommand.capnp_executable()`.
- Remove obsolete `RustEdition` enum.
##v0.12.3-Generate code for new capnp::capability::FromServer trait.
##v0.12.2-Add `parentModule` annotation to allow generated code to be included in a submodule.
##v0.12.1-Add rust.capnp file with `name` annotation for renaming items in generated Rust code.
##v0.12.0-Remove deprecated item.
##v0.11.1-Avoid generating some superfluous parentheses.
##v0.11.0-Remove unused experimental `schema` module.
- Bump minimum supported rustc version to 1.39.0.
##v0.10.2-Include the string "@generated" generated code.
- Don't write output files if their content is unchanged.
##v0.10.1-Allow CompilerCommand to work even when OUT_DIR is not set.
##v0.10.0-Simplify handling of pointer defaults.
- Use new const fn ::capnp::word() instead of capnp_word!() macro.
- Remove deprecated items.
- Use dyn keyword for trait objects.
- Deprecate edition() configuration. Apparently the code we generate for Rust 2018 also works for Rust 2015 now.
- Update to 2018 edition.
- Update minimum required rustc version to 1.35.
##v0.9.5-Fix bug in code generation for generic interfaces.
##v0.9.4-Add support for pointer field defaults.
##v0.9.3-Generate impls of new IntoInternalStructReader trait, to support set_with_caveats.
- Update deprecation attributes, to satisfy clippy.
##v0.9.2-Rename a bunch of as_reader() methods to into_reader(), to satisfy clippy.
##v0.9.1-Add support for Rust 2018.
- Fix a bunch of clippy warnings.
##v0.9.0-Remove deprecated items.
##v0.8.9-Deprecate borrow() in favor of reborrow().
##v0.8.8-Support List(Interface).
##v0.8.7-Eliminate `use` statements in generated code to avoid naming conflicts.
##v0.8.6-Improve error message for snake_case method names.
- Eliminate floating point literals in match statements.
##v0.8.5-Implement enum defaults.
- Emit "UNIMPLEMENTED" warnings on struct and list defaults.
##v0.8.4-Implement struct, list, and enum constants.
##v0.8.3-Fix bug where schemas with non-trivial relative filesystem paths could fail to compile.
##v0.8.2-Fix bug where `initn_*()` methods of generic unions failed to set the discriminant.
##v0.8.1-Fix several formatting issues in generated code.
- Remove some unneccesary trait bounds in generated code.
- Add `import_path()` and `no_std_import()` options to `CompilerCommand`.
##v0.8.0-Remove deprecated `compile()` and `compile_with_src_prefixes()` functions.
##v0.7.5-Fix bug that prevented compilation of interfaces with generic superclasses.
- More robust error handling.
##v0.7.4-Deprecate `compile()` and `compile_with_src_prefixes()` in favor of `CompilerCommand`.
##v0.7.3-`capnpc -orust ./foo/bar/baz.capnp` now correctly writes to `./foo/bar/baz_capnp.rs` rather than
just `./baz_capnp.rs`. If you were depending on the old behavior you can use the `--src-prefix`flag for finer-grained control of the output location.
##v0.7.2-Nicer formatting for floating point literals.
##v0.7.1-Fix bug that prevented pipelining on an AnyPointer field.

# capnpc 0.26.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnpc/latest/source/README.md

```
[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/capnpc.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/capnpc)
[documentation](https://docs.rs/capnpc/)
The generated code depends on the [capnproto-rust runtime library](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust).
Code generation can be customized through the annotations defined in [`rust.capnp`](rust.capnp).
```

---

# capnpc 0.26.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnpc/latest/source/rust.capnp

```
# This file contains annotations that are recognized by the capnpc-rust code generator.
#
# To use this file, you will need to make sure that it is included in the directories
# searched by `capnp compile`. An easy way to do that is to copy it into your project
# alongside your own schema files.
@0x83b3c14c3c8dd083;
annotation name @0xc2fe4c6d100166d0 (field, struct, enum, enumerant, union, group) :Text;
# Rename something in the generated code. The value that you specify in this
# annotation should follow capnp capitalization conventions. So, for example,
# a struct should use CamelCase capitalization like `StructFoo`, even though
# that will get translated to a `struct_foo` module in the generated Rust code.
#
# TODO: support annotating more kinds of things with this.
annotation parentModule @0xabee386cd1450364 (file) :Text;
# A Rust module path indicating where the generated code will be included.
# For example, if this is set to "foo::bar" and the schema file is named
# "baz.capnp", then you could include the generated code like this:
#
#  pub mod foo {
#    pub mod bar {
#      capnp::generated_code!(pub mod baz_capnp);
#    }
#  }
annotation option @0xabfef22c4ee1964e (field) :Void;
# Make the generated getters return Option<T> instead of T. Supported on
# pointer types (e.g. structs, lists, and blobs).
#
# Capnp pointer types are nullable. Normally get_field will return the default
# value if the field isn't set. With this annotation you get Some(...) when
# the field is set and None when it isn't.
#
# Given
#
#     struct Test {
#         field @0 :Text $Rust.option;
#     }
#
# you get getters like so
#
#     assert_eq!(struct_with.get_field(), Some("foo"));
#     assert_eq!(struct_without.get_field(), None));
#
# The setters are unchanged to match the Rust convention.
#
# Note: Support for this annotation on interfaces isn't implemented yet.
```
